title: A brief history of Italian: how one city’s dialect became a nation’s language
summary: From the language of the Romans to a diverse collection of dialects, learn what shaped the 2,500-year history of Italian.
body_markdown:
[Italian](https://blog.duolingo.com/italian-pronunciation-guide/) is the language of opera and the Renaissance, of Dante and Fellini, of *la dolce vita* . Even if you’ve never studied it,[you already speak a little](https://blog.duolingo.com/italian-fun-facts/) : *ciao* ,[pizza](https://blog.duolingo.com/how-to-order-food-in-italian/) , *piano* , *paparazzi* , and plenty more!


But here’s a surprising fact: when Italy became a single country in 1861, only a small fraction of its citizens actually spoke Italian! Everyone else spoke Neapolitan, Venetian, Sicilian, Sardinian, or one (or more) of dozens of other local languages.


So how did Italian become the[standard language](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-standardization/) of a whole nation? The story involves an empire, a few invasions, a lot of poetry, a dictionary named after flour bran, and, believe it or not, television. Andiamo!


Here is what you’ll find in this post:


- Where did Italian come from?
- After Rome: new rulers, new words
- From a monk’s riddle to Dante
- The Renaissance: rules, bran, and Italian
- 1861: Italy is made, now for the Italians


## Where did Italian come from?


Like[French](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-french/) ,[Spanish](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-spanish/) and[many more](https://blog.duolingo.com/what-are-romance-languages/#there-are-more-than-a-dozen-romance-languages-still-spoken-today) , Italian is a[Romance language](https://blog.duolingo.com/what-are-romance-languages/) , which means it evolved from Latin—the language of ancient Rome. But Latin wasn’t always the language of Italy!


About 2,500 years ago, the Italian peninsula was full of different languages, like Etruscan (in central Italy), Greek (in the southern colonies), Oscan (in the south, including Pompeii), Umbrian (in today’s Umbria), Venetic (in the northeast), and Celtic languages (in the north, brought by the Gauls). Latin started out as the language of one small region, Latium (today’s Lazio), and one ambitious city: Rome. As Rome grew more powerful, Latin[spread across the whole peninsula](https://blog.duolingo.com/what-are-romance-languages/#romance-languages-started-with-latin) (and beyond), and most of the other languages gave way to regional varieties of Latin,[each colored a little by the languages spoken there before](https://blog.duolingo.com/language-evolution-in-history/) .


## After Rome: new rulers, new words


When the Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE, Italy broke into many pieces, and it wouldn’t be a single country again for almost 1,400 years. Over those centuries, different groups ruled different parts of the peninsula, and each one left some words behind.


**The Lombards (6th–8th centuries)**
The Lombards, a Germanic people, arrived in 568 CE and ruled much of Italy for about two centuries. The northern region of Lombardia is still named after them! Germanic speakers like the Lombards gave Italian some highly frequent words, such as guancia


(cheek), schiena


(back) and zaino


(backpack).


**The Arabs in Sicily (9th–11th centuries)**
For more than two centuries, Sicily was ruled by Arabic-speaking Muslims, and it became a center of farming, science, and trade. Many Arabic words entered Sicilian and, from there, Italian, for example zibibbo


(a type of grape and sweet wine) from زبيب


( *zabiib* , raisins), albicocca


(apricot) from البرقوق


( *al-barquuq* , apricot), and sciabica


(fishing net) from شبكة


( *shabaka* , net).


**The Normans and Frederick II (11th–13th centuries)**
Yes, these are the same Normans who[conquered England in 1066](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-english-language/#middle-english) ! Around the same time, they took over Sicily and southern Italy. Their royal court in Palermo became wonderfully multilingual, with Latin, Greek, Arabic, and Sicilian all in the mix. That tradition continued under Frederick II, the Normans’ Hohenstaufen heir, whose court poets began writing love poems in Sicilian instead of Latin. This was the start of Italian poetry!


So by the 1200s, Italy was a patchwork of local Romance varieties, each flavored by whoever had ruled the area, while almost everything important was still written in Latin. Which of those many varieties would become “Italian” was still an open question, and the first written traces of the answer appear much earlier than you might think.


## From a monk’s riddle to Dante


Rewind to around the year 800 CE, when a monk in Verona scribbled a short riddle in the margin of a prayer book. Known today as the Indovinello veronese


(Veronese riddle), it’s mostly Latin, but with some words that already sound like the everyday speech around him. The riddle describes someone “plowing a white field” and “sowing black seed”—the answer is a person writing with a quill pen!


A century and a half later came the document most often called Italian’s “birth certificate”: the Placito Capuano


, a legal record from 960 CE about land owned by the monastery of Montecassino. Most of it is in Latin, but the witnesses’ sworn testimony was written in the local vernacular so ordinary people could understand exactly what they were swearing to.


Placito Capuano (960 CE) Modern Italian English


*Sao ko kelle terre, per kelle fini que ki contene, trenta anni le possette parte Sancti Benedicti.* *So che quelle terre, entro quei confini che qui sono descritti, le ha possedute per trent’anni la parte di San Benedetto.* I know that those lands, within the borders described here, were owned for thirty years by the party of Saint Benedict.


Notice how *sao* is the ancestor of modern so


(I know), *kelle* is an old spelling of quelle


(those), and trenta anni


(thirty years) hasn’t changed!


But the first real literature in an Italian vernacular came from that multilingual court in Palermothat I mentioned above . In the 1200s, poets there wrote love poetry in a polished Sicilian, and one of them, Giacomo da Lentini, is credited with inventing the sonetto


, or *little song* . Yes, the sonnet—Shakespeare’s favorite form started out in Sicily!


Still, the variety that won the race was Florentine, from Tuscany. Florence was rich (its gold coin, the *florin* , was used all over Europe), full of merchants who read and wrote, and home to three writers Italians still call le tre corone


(the three crowns): Dante, Petrarch, and Boccaccio.


Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), often called the father of the Italian language, made a bold choice in his Commedia


(later renamed Divina Commedia


, or *Divine Comedy* ): Instead of writing in Latin like a serious scholar, he wrote in Florentine, the language people actually spoke!


Dante was followed by Petrarch (1304–1374), whose love sonnets were imitated all over Europe, and Boccaccio (1313–1375), whose Decameron


—100 stories told by young Florentines hiding out from the plague—became a model for Italian prose.


Thanks to these three, Florentine (also called Tuscan more generally) became the most admired written vernacular in Italy, but it still wasn’t a real standard—in the 1400s, many scholars went back to writing in Latin, and those who wrote in the vernacular often mixed Tuscan with their own local speech. And, perhaps more importantly, Tuscan wasn’t *spoken* outside of Tuscany.


## The Renaissance: rules, bran, and Italian


By the 1500s, writers were debating what standard Italian should even be. The winning answer came from the Venetian scholar Pietro Bembo, who argued in 1525 that everyone should follow the Florentine of Petrarch and Boccaccio—a model that was already 200 years old!


Then in 1583, a group of Florentine friends founded the Accademia della Crusca


, with the goal of defining and standardizing the Italian language. *Crusca* means *bran* , the husk you sift out of flour, because the academy wanted to separate the “good” words from the “bad” ones. Finally, in 1612, it published one of the very first dictionaries of a modern European language—a century before Spain’s[Real Academia Española](https://blog.duolingo.com/history-of-spanish/#modern-spanish-keeps-changing-and-innovating) was even founded.


## 1861: Italy is made, now for the Italians


When Italy unified in 1861, only a small portion of people in Italy actually spoke Italian (between around 2.5% and 10% of the population). A farmer from Sicily and a farmer from Veneto would not have been able to communicate very easily! A saying often attributed to the politician Massimo d’Azeglio summed it up: Fatta l’Italia, bisogna fare gli italiani


(Now that we’ve made Italy, we need to make Italians).


But just how different were these languages? They all grew out of Latin, but over more than a thousand years, each one went its own way, and they’re still very much alive. Here’s how a few everyday words compare in these languages today:


Neapolitan Venetian Sicilian
(Palermitano) Sardinian
(Logudorese) Standard
Italian Translation


Jamme! Ndemo! Amunì! Ajò! Andiamo! Let’s go!


Che? Cossa? Chi? Ite? Che / (Che) cosa? What?


guaglione toso picciottu pitzinnu ragazzo boy


dimane doman dumani cras domani tomorrow


All these languages share Latin roots, but with different results! For example, Sardinian *cras* (tomorrow) is the exact same as the Latin word, with the same meaning! You know it from *pro **cras** tinate* : in other words, “putting things off until *cras* ” 😉 The rest of those languages got their word for *tomorrow* from Latin *de mane* (literally, *in the morning* ).


So how do you get millions of people to share one language? One writer had a head start. Alessandro Manzoni, from Milan, wasn’t happy with the Lombard-flavored language of his novel I promessi sposi


(The Betrothed), so he moved to Florence to “rinse his clothes in the Arno,” Florence’s river, and rewrote it in Florentine. The final version (1840–42) became a model for modern Italian prose, and students still read it today.


After unification, written and spoken Italian spread through schools, military service that mixed young men from every region, migration to big cities, and television! When RAI, Italy’s national public broadcaster, began regular TV broadcasts in 1954, Italians everywhere heard the same Italian every night, and a show called Non è mai troppo tardi


(It’s never too late) even taught huge numbers of adults how to read and write.


Today, Italian has more than 60 million first-language speakers and is an official language in Italy, San Marino, Vatican City, and Switzerland. Many Italians still speak a regional language alongside it. Italian also traveled far beyond Italy, from Buenos Aires to Malta, but that’s a story for another post!


## The story continues…


From Latin to the standard language of today, Italian picked up something from every chapter of its history, and it’s still growing. Every word you learn connects you to a thousand years of poets, merchants, monks, and TV hosts 📺✨ So the next time you say ciao


, remember you’re part of the story too. Forza, continua così!


(Come on, keep it up!) 💚
